opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a real risk, and I think about it a lot. These models are trained to be helpful, and in practice that often means agreeable. If you come in with a half-formed idea and frame it a certain way, the model tends to pick up on that framing and run with it. It'll give you reasons why you're right, sometimes very eloquently, and that can feel like validation when it's really just an echo.

So I try to use them almost adversarially. Instead of asking "here's my idea, help me develop it," I'll ask "here's my idea, tell me why it's wrong" or "what would a smart skeptic say about this?" Or I'll argue the opposite position and see how the model responds. If it's equally enthusiastic about both sides, that tells you something: it's reflecting you back, not giving you independent judgment.

The other thing is that I don't treat it as the final word. It's a great thinking partner for getting a first draft of an argument out or surfacing angles I hadn't considered, but the real test is still talking to people: customers, engineers, folks on my team who'll push back. Humans with skin in the game will tell you when you're wrong in a way a chatbot often won't.

And I think this matters more broadly as these tools become part of how everyone thinks and works. If millions of people are using systems that gently confirm whatever they already believe, that's a societal problem, not just a personal productivity issue. So I'd like to see the model builders put more emphasis on calibrated disagreement, models that are comfortable saying "I don't think that's right, and here's why." That's what makes a good advisor, human or machine.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think about this a lot, because I use these tools every day, and I'm acutely aware that they're designed to be agreeable. If I go to a chatbot and say, "Here's my thesis, help me build the case," it will happily build the case. It won't push back unless I explicitly ask it to, and even then, it tends to soften the pushback. So the risk is very real. You end up with a very articulate, very polished version of what you already believed, and you walk away more confident without actually being more right.

What I try to do is treat it less like a collaborator and more like a sparring partner that I have to provoke. I'll ask it to argue the opposite position as forcefully as it can. I'll ask it what a skeptical investor or a competitor would say about an idea. I'll ask it where the reasoning is weakest. And you have to be a little disciplined about this, because the natural pull is to stop when the answer feels good.

The other thing I'd say is that in hardware, in what we do at d-Matrix, reality is a very good corrective. You can convince yourself of anything in a document, but silicon doesn't care about your narrative. A chip either hits the power envelope or it doesn't. So I'm fortunate that the feedback loop from the physical world keeps me honest in a way that a chatbot never will.

But for people working purely in the world of ideas, I do worry. These models reflect you back to yourself with remarkable fluency, and fluency is very easy to mistake for truth. The responsibility is on the user to go looking for the disagreement, because the tool is not going to volunteer it.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real risk, because you can walk away from a conversation feeling that your idea has been validated when, in fact, the model has just followed the framing you gave it. If your question already contains an assumption, the answer may build on that assumption rather than challenge it.

So I think you have to be deliberate about how you use it. Ask, “What’s wrong with this argument? What’s the strongest case against it? What evidence would change my mind?” Use it as a way to explore opposing views, and then test those views against evidence and people who disagree with you.

It can be a very useful thinking partner, but agreement from a chatbot isn’t independent confirmation that you’re right.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real risk. If you come in with a strong point of view and frame your questions around it, you can end up getting a very articulate version of what you already believe. And because it sounds thoughtful, you may mistake that for independent validation.

So I think you have to deliberately ask for pushback: What am I missing? What’s the strongest argument against this? What evidence would change my mind? That makes it a more useful tool for developing ideas. But you still have to bring your own judgment and test those ideas with people who don’t necessarily agree with you.
